Issues.Title: Kestrel HTTP/2 performs only two of the four field validations RFC 9113 8.2.1 requires: a space or a colon in a header name, and leading or trailing whitespace in a value, are accepted
Issues.Body:
### Is there an existing issue for this?

I searched open and closed issues here for HTTP/2 header name validation, field name tokens, colons in header names, and leading or trailing whitespace in field values, and did not find this reported. The nearest one I found is #69574, which is about the connection-specific header list rather than field name and field value characters.

### Describe the bug

RFC 9113 §8.2.1 lists four minimal validations an HTTP/2 implementation MUST perform on field names and values. Kestrel performs two of them and not the other two.

It rejects uppercase field names, and it rejects NUL, LF and CR inside a field value. It accepts:

* a field name containing an ASCII space, which §8.2.1 forbids as part of the range 0x00-0x20,
* a field name containing a colon,
* a field value that starts or ends with an ASCII space.

The spec's wording on the last two:

> With the exception of pseudo-header fields (Section 8.3), which have a name that starts with a single colon, field names MUST NOT include a colon (ASCII COLON, 0x3a).

> A field value MUST NOT start or end with an ASCII whitespace character (ASCII SP or HTAB, 0x20 or 0x09).

and the consequence it attaches to all four bullets:

> A request or response that contains a field that violates any of these conditions MUST be treated as malformed (Section 8.1.1).

The same section says why the colon is on that list:

> Failure to validate fields can be exploited for request smuggling attacks. In particular, unvalidated fields might enable attacks when messages are forwarded using HTTP/1.1 [HTTP/1.1], where characters such as carriage return (CR), line feed (LF), and COLON are used as delimiters.

CR and LF are the two that Kestrel does reject. COLON is in the same sentence and is accepted.

### Measured behaviour

A minimal app whose handler reports the header name and value it was handed, byte for byte, with Kestrel listening for HTTP/1.1 on one loopback port and HTTP/2 cleartext on another. The HTTP/2 requests come from a raw client using HPACK literal-never-indexed with no Huffman coding, so the bytes on the wire are exactly the bytes in the table.

| what the client sends | HTTP/1.1 | HTTP/2 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `x-probe: AB` (control) | name `x-probe`, value `AB` | name `x-probe`, value `AB` |
| `x:probe: AB` | name `x`, value `probe: AB` | name `x:probe`, value `AB` |
| `x probe: AB` | **400 Bad Request** | name `x probe`, value `AB` |
| `x-probe:  AB` (extra leading space) | value `AB` | value ` AB` |
| `x-probe: AB ` (trailing space) | value `AB` | value `AB ` |

The control agrees on both protocols, so the two paths are being measured consistently. The three HTTP/2 rows are identical on 10.0.14 and on 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148, so this is not something the .NET 11 work already covered.

The `x:probe` row is the smuggling shape the spec describes, demonstrated inside one server: those bytes mean a header named `x` with the value `probe: AB` to Kestrel's HTTP/1.1 parser, and a header named `x:probe` with the value `AB` to its HTTP/2 parser.

### Where it comes from

`Http2Connection.ValidateHeaderContent` checks the name for uppercase letters and nothing else:

```csharp
private void ValidateHeaderContent(ReadOnlySpan<byte> name, ReadOnlySpan<byte> value)
{
    // A request or response containing uppercase header field names MUST be treated as malformed
    for (var i = 0; i < name.Length; i++)
    {
        if (((uint)name[i] - 65) <= (90 - 65))
        {
            ...
        }
    }
}
```

§8.2.1 carries a note that explains how this came to be the only check:

> Note: An implementation that validates fields according to the definitions in Sections 5.1 and 5.5 of [HTTP] only needs an additional check that field names do not include uppercase characters.

The uppercase check is that additional check. What is missing is the base validation it is meant to be added to.

`Http3Stream.ValidateHeaderContent` has the same shape, so I expect HTTP/3 to behave the same way, but I measured HTTP/2 only and would rather not claim HTTP/3 without measuring it.

### Why it matters, and what it is not

Kestrel as the origin server does not misframe anything here. The body comes from DATA frames, and I measured no framing divergence.

What does change is what the application is handed. Code that compares a header value as a string sees `" AB"` over HTTP/2 where it sees `"AB"` over HTTP/1.1, from identical client bytes. Code that forwards the request to an HTTP/1.1 hop has to re-serialize a name that is not a token, and `x:probe: AB` on an HTTP/1.1 request becomes a different header with a different value, as the table above shows Kestrel's own HTTP/1.1 parser doing.

I am not reporting a remotely exploitable vulnerability in Kestrel itself. I am reporting that two of the four MUST validations in §8.2.1 are absent, that one of the two missing ones is the character the spec singles out for smuggling when messages are forwarded over HTTP/1.1, and that the result is a protocol-dependent view of the same header.

### Expected behaviour

A field name containing a space or a colon, and a field value starting or ending with a space, are treated as malformed on HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, the same way an uppercase field name already is and the same way Kestrel's HTTP/1.1 path already rejects a name that is not a token.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Run an app with Kestrel listening with `HttpProtocols.Http1` on one loopback port and `HttpProtocols.Http2` on another, whose handler writes `Request.Headers` out as hex so a changed value cannot look like an unchanged one.
2. Send `GET /x HTTP/1.1` with the header line `x probe: AB` to the HTTP/1.1 port. It answers 400 Bad Request.
3. Send the same name and value over HTTP/2 to the other port, as an HPACK literal-never-indexed field with no Huffman coding. It answers 200 and the application sees a header named `x probe`.
4. Repeat with the name `x:probe`, and with a value that has a leading or a trailing space, comparing the two ports each time.

### Exceptions (if any)

_No response_

### .NET Version

10.0.14 and 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148, Linux x86_64

### Anything else?

Both rows of the table were taken on both runtimes. The HTTP/2 behaviour did not differ between them.

Issues.Title: .NET 11 regression: malformed linker XML in Components.Endpoints causes IL2101 during trimmed publishing
Issues.Body:
### Describe the bug

`Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Endpoints` embeds an `ILLink.Substitutions.xml` resource whose assembly `fullname` incorrectly targets `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Forms`. This causes IL2101 during trimmed publishing.

This affects trimmed publishing of Blazor applications and can also occur in non-Blazor applications. A console application referencing `Microsoft.AspNetCore.App` and using `IHtmlHelper` reproduces the problem without RazorSlices, Razor files, MVC services, or Blazor registration.

When IL2101 is treated as an error, publishing fails with NETSDK1144.

### Expected Behavior

The embedded linker XML targets the correct assembly, and the application publishes without IL2101, as it does with .NET 10.

### Steps To Reproduce

Using .NET SDK `11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148`, create a console application with these files.

**Repro.csproj**
```xml
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <OutputType>Exe</OutputType>
    <TargetFramework>net11.0</TargetFramework>
  </PropertyGroup>
  <ItemGroup>
    <FrameworkReference Include="Microsoft.AspNetCore.App" />
  </ItemGroup>
</Project>
```

**Program.cs**
```csharp
System.Console.WriteLine(
    typeof(Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Rendering.IHtmlHelper).FullName);
```

Publish with trimming enabled:
```powershell
dotnet publish -c Release -r win-x64 --self-contained true -p:PublishAot=false -p:PublishTrimmed=true -p:ILLinkTreatWarningsAsErrors=false
```

Observe IL2101 for the embedded `ILLink.Substitutions.xml` resource in `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Endpoints`.

Repeat with `-p:ILLinkTreatWarningsAsErrors=true` to observe publishing fail with NETSDK1144.

### Exceptions (if any)

IL2101 reports malformed linker XML. Treating the warning as an error causes NETSDK1144.

### .NET Version

Reported with SDK `11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148`.

The equivalent `net10.0` reproduction using SDK `10.0.403` and runtime/linker packs `10.0.14` does not emit IL2101.

### Anything else?

According to Damian's investigation:

- ViewFeatures leads the linker to Components.Endpoints. Its XML is parsed even though Endpoints is unmarked and removed from the final output.
- The malformed resource was introduced by commit `309d909185` in #65903 and remained incorrect on the inspected `main` snapshot.
- The .NET 10 linker already performs the cross-assembly XML check, so this is a framework resource regression rather than a new linker diagnostic.

This issue isolates the IL2101 problem described in #69270 and tracks its impact on both Blazor and non-Blazor applications.

**Proposed servicing target:** the first .NET 11 servicing window in December, subject to servicing approval.

Issues.Title: [Review agent] False positive: unsupported-concurrency race in AuthorizationMessageHandler on #70106
Issues.Body:
### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### Describe the bug

The hosted `/review` agent published a P2 concurrency finding on [#70106](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/70106#discussion_r4431751648). It claimed that `NotifyAuthenticationStateChanged`, raised on another thread, can interleave between the cancellation check and the cache write in `AuthorizationMessageHandler.SendAsync` and cache a stale token.

At the reviewed head, the check and both cache writes are synchronous: no `await` falls between them. Blazor WebAssembly runs single-threaded, so the claimed interleaving requires multithreaded execution that is not a supported configuration. The finding was later withdrawn on the PR. This tracks a **review-agent failure**, not an authentication product bug.

- Hosted run: [41202500880](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/actions/runs/41202500880).
- Reviewed head: `2edf3761692afe15475075eb2fc0088566162045`.
- Reviewer/guidance revision: `4f556f73a610b386e5ec29355a300e493d30c4c5`; observed model: `gpt-5.6-sol`.
- Verdict: **Wrong for supported configurations**. The race is reachable only under unsupported multithreaded execution.

### Expected Behavior

A race finding should be accepted only after it identifies a supported caller or producer that actually schedules both operations concurrently. That a host or runtime is capable of threading shows the code can be reached, not that the two operations overlap.

The two routed guide workers disagreed here: Cross-Cutting reported the candidate and Blazor Components reported nothing. The coordinator resolved the disagreement by accepting the candidate. When re-checking does not settle the trigger and causal path, the skill already requires recording the candidate as `UNRESOLVED` ([SKILL.md:213-215](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/4f556f73a610b386e5ec29355a300e493d30c4c5/.github/skills/review-pull-request/SKILL.md#L213-L215)).

### Steps To Reproduce

This is reproducible from the retained review and immutable source; no new reviewer dispatch is needed.

1. Read the [published finding](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/70106#discussion_r4431751648) and the [review summary](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/70106#pullrequestreview-5722771822), which records the worker disagreement.
2. At the reviewed head, inspect [AuthorizationMessageHandler.cs:71-81](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/2edf3761692afe15475075eb2fc0088566162045/src/Components/WebAssembly/WebAssembly.Authentication/src/Services/AuthorizationMessageHandler.cs#L71-L81). The only interleaving points are the `RequestAccessToken` awaits, which the authentication-state `CancellationTokenSource` already covers. The check at line 77 and the writes at lines 79-80 run without yielding.
3. See the [author reply](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/70106#discussion_r4431799752) and the [follow-up review](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/70106#pullrequestreview-5723402763). The ordering reproduced only under genuinely multithreaded execution, which current Blazor WebAssembly does not support, so the finding was withdrawn.

### Exceptions (if any)

None. The published repro needs a second thread to run the callback while the handler is paused between two synchronous statements. That cannot happen on the supported single-threaded runtime.

### .NET Version

N/A for reproducing this reviewer failure from saved output and source.

### Anything else?

Parent tracking epic: [#70231](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/70231).

Exploratory evidence from one published finding; this does not estimate general reviewer accuracy. In offline replays of this same claim, reviewers repeatedly justified acceptance by "the host supports multithreading" rather than by a concrete concurrent producer. Candidate skill changes for this pattern are being evaluated locally, with real-race sentinels to avoid suppressing valid concurrency findings.

Issues.Body:
# Fix RDG handling of failed form antiforgery validation

<!-- Thank you for submitting a pull request to our repo. -->

<!-- If this is your first PR in the ASP.NET Core repo, please run through the checklist
below to ensure a smooth review and merge process for your PR. -->

- [ ] You've read the [Contributor Guide](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CODE-OF-CONDUCT.md).
- [x] You've included unit or integration tests for your change, where applicable.
- [ ] You've included inline docs for your change, where applicable.
- [x] There's an open issue for the PR that you are making. If you'd like to propose a new feature or change, please open an issue to discuss the change or find an existing issue.

<!-- Once all that is done, you're ready to go. Open the PR with the content below. -->

Return HTTP 400 for failed antiforgery validation in generated form binding.

## Description

RDG's generated `TryResolveFormAsync` accesses `HttpRequest.HasFormContentType` without first checking `IAntiforgeryValidationFeature`. When middleware records a failed validation, `FormFeature` throws `InvalidOperationException` from that property access, producing HTTP 500 instead of the HTTP 400 returned by runtime `RequestDelegateFactory`.

Check the validation result before form access and use the existing shared antiforgery diagnostic messages to match RDF's Debug logging and `ThrowOnBadRequest` behavior. Valid requests continue to bind normally. No public API changes.

Regression coverage executes both generated and runtime delegates through the real automatic validation or token-validation middleware. It covers cross-site requests, same-site requests with mismatched Origin, Origin fallback, missing and invalid tokens, valid tokens without matching cookies, and valid controls. Token failures also verify handler suppression, the logged exception, and `BadHttpRequestException` when configured to throw.

The logging helper is emitted in all existing generator snapshots, so all 53 baselines were regenerated using the existing harness; only the form-binding baseline additionally changes its form helper.

### Validation

Reproduced against current `main` at `4f556f73a610b386e5ec29355a300e493d30c4c5`: all nine RDG rejection cases failed with the reported `InvalidOperationException`, while the equivalent RDF cases and valid controls passed. After the fix, all 22 focused cases passed.

Final validation, from the repository root:

```powershell
. .\activate.ps1
$env:ASPNETCORE_TEST_LOG_MAXPATH = '32767'
dotnet test .\src\Http\Http.Extensions\test\Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http.Extensions.Tests.csproj --no-restore -p:BuildNodeJS=false -p:UseIisNativeAssets=false --filter "FullyQualifiedName~Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http.Generators.Tests" --logger "trx;LogFileName=rdg-antiforgery.trx" --results-directory 'C:\Users\dedward\.copilot\session-state\2e77c8e1-6e14-45a9-b55a-cc8f0333d8aa\files\test-results' -v:q
```

Result: **1,678 passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped**, exit code 0. Parsed the TRX and confirmed all 22 regression cases passed. The command uses the repository's current net12.0 SDK/runtime; it does not independently verify the fix on the released .NET 10/11 runtimes. Node.js and IIS native assets are excluded because these tests do not exercise those boundaries. Inline documentation is not applicable to this internal bug fix.

Fixes #70229

Issues.Title: [Review agent] Incorrect instrument-duplication claim and ineffective test fix on #70174
Issues.Body:
### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### Describe the bug

The hosted `/review` agent published a P3 finding on [#70174](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/70174#discussion_r4436520149), claiming that reverting Identity metrics-wrapper caching leaves duplicate instrument creation unprotected. It recommends counting instrument publications to make the regression tests detect that reversion.

**The test-coverage premise is partly true:** the new output/measurement tests do not assert that the metrics wrapper is cached. **The material consequence and proposed remedy are wrong:** the real `Meter` already caches matching counters/histograms. The sequential tests would still publish one instrument per matching metric when wrapper caching is removed, so the proposed assertion would also pass without the optimization.

This tracks a **review-agent failure**, not a demonstrated Identity behavior defect.

- Hosted run: [41328306988](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/actions/runs/41328306988).
- Reviewed head: `5c5d461e4067b8a47e88e2b6b80d7112020d8805`.
- Reviewer/guidance revision: `4f556f73a610b386e5ec29355a300e493d30c4c5`; observed model: `gpt-5.6-sol`.
- Verdict: **Wrong for its material consequence/remedy**, with the partly true premise retained. No author acceptance, disagreement, or fix was present when last checked.

### Expected Behavior

Separate tests preserving observable compatibility from tests proving an allocation/construction optimization. A test passing without an optimization does not establish duplicate instrument publication.

Trace the real producer contract before recommending an assertion, and establish that the suggested assertion distinguishes the intended change. If necessary runtime implementation is outside the frozen bundle, keep the dependent claim unresolved, as required by [pull-request-review.md:394-397](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/4f556f73a610b386e5ec29355a300e493d30c4c5/.github/workflows/pull-request-review.md#L394-L397).

A useful report could accurately note that wrapper caching is not directly asserted, without inventing duplicate instruments or prescribing an ineffective publication-count assertion.

### Steps To Reproduce

Use the retained finding and immutable source; no new reviewer dispatch is needed.

1. Read the [published finding](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/70174#discussion_r4436520149).
2. Inspect the new shared-factory tests at the reviewed head: [UserManagerTest](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/5c5d461e4067b8a47e88e2b6b80d7112020d8805/src/Identity/test/Identity.Test/UserManagerTest.cs#L153-L175) and [SignInManagerTest](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/5c5d461e4067b8a47e88e2b6b80d7112020d8805/src/Identity/test/Identity.Test/SignInManagerTest.cs#L1784-L1805). Both construct/use the managers sequentially and assert measurement counts and one Meter.
3. Follow [TestMeterFactory.Create:15-27](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/5c5d461e4067b8a47e88e2b6b80d7112020d8805/src/Shared/Metrics/TestMeterFactory.cs#L15-L27): repeated matching requests return the same real `Meter`.
4. Inspect [UserManagerMetrics](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/5c5d461e4067b8a47e88e2b6b80d7112020d8805/src/Identity/Extensions.Core/src/UserManagerMetrics.cs#L35-L81) and [SignInManagerMetrics](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/5c5d461e4067b8a47e88e2b6b80d7112020d8805/src/Identity/Core/src/SignInManagerMetrics.cs#L31-L80). Repeated construction uses identical metric names/types/units/descriptions/tags; the added comments explicitly state that instruments are cached per Meter and identify the optimization as caching the wrapper instance.
5. Inspect [dotnet/runtime Meter.cs at f368d14d:526-563](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/f368d14df0c3905d3b80073d709685af83ba895d/src/libraries/System.Diagnostics.DiagnosticSource/src/System/Diagnostics/Metrics/Meter.cs#L526-L563). `GetOrCreateInstrument` returns an existing matching instrument before invoking the creator. The same caching contract was also checked at [v10.0.0 / 60629d14](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/60629d14374c56f1cb51819049ad1fa529307f8d/src/libraries/System.Diagnostics.DiagnosticSource/src/System/Diagnostics/Metrics/Meter.cs).

Under these sequential inputs, a publication-count assertion remains one with or without wrapper caching. It therefore does not protect the optimization the reviewer says it would protect.

### Exceptions (if any)

N/A. The observed failure is an incorrect published explanation and ineffective proposed test assertion.

### .NET Version

The reviewed repository targets `net12.0`. Adjudication is source-only: current runtime source was pinned to `f368d14df0c3905d3b80073d709685af83ba895d`, and the caching implementation was cross-checked at v10.0.0. The exact net12 runtime build used by the PR was not inspected or executed; no test-pass or mutation-test result is claimed.

### Anything else?

Parent tracking epic: [#70231](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/70231).

The published finding's valid coverage observation and invalid consequence/remedy should remain separate in evaluation records. This is exploratory evidence from one run, not a general accuracy measurement.

The run retained a complete structured coordinator result before publication; its later prose confirmation is not itself evidence of a missing structured result. The improvement here is causal validation and useful test recommendations, not terminal-message formatting.

Issues.Title: [Review agent] False positive: MessagePack count validation ignored on #70143
Issues.Body:
### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### Describe the bug

The hosted `/review` agent published a wrong P2 finding on [#70143](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/70143#discussion_r4436130891), claiming an `array32` stream-ID header declaring millions of elements with no payload reaches `new string[streamIdCount]` and causes a count-sized allocation.

The pinned MessagePack reader rejects that input before returning the array count. The claimed allocation is unreachable for the published repro, and the suggested remaining-payload check duplicates existing validation. This tracks a **review-agent failure**, not a SignalR product bug.

- Hosted run: [41318073313](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/actions/runs/41318073313).
- Reviewed head: `d6c5bb8a057f8f608dbf4210fc556a73b14418e9`.
- Reviewer/guidance revision: `4f556f73a610b386e5ec29355a300e493d30c4c5`; observed model: `gpt-5.6-sol`.
- Verdict: **Wrong**, adjudicated against source rather than author disagreement alone.

### Expected Behavior

Before publishing, trace the called external contract needed to establish reachability. If necessary dependency implementation is absent from the frozen bundle, retain the candidate as unresolved instead of assuming it. This is already required by [pull-request-review.md:394-397](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/4f556f73a610b386e5ec29355a300e493d30c4c5/.github/workflows/pull-request-review.md#L394-L397).

For this case, the documented malformed input should not be reported as reaching the allocation. Do not recommend a duplicate guard as its fix.

### Steps To Reproduce

This is reproducible from the retained review and immutable source; no new reviewer dispatch is needed.

1. Read the [published finding](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/70143#discussion_r4436130891) and its malformed `array32` input.
2. At the reviewed head, follow [the stream-ID count/allocation path](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/d6c5bb8a057f8f608dbf4210fc556a73b14418e9/src/SignalR/common/Protocols.MessagePack/src/Protocol/MessagePackHubProtocolWorker.cs#L265-L275) into [ReadArrayLength](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/d6c5bb8a057f8f608dbf4210fc556a73b14418e9/src/SignalR/common/Protocols.MessagePack/src/Protocol/MessagePackHubProtocolWorker.cs#L714-L718).
3. Confirm [eng/Versions.props](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/d6c5bb8a057f8f608dbf4210fc556a73b14418e9/eng/Versions.props#L168) pins MessagePack 2.5.303.
4. Inspect [MessagePack-CSharp/MessagePack-CSharp ReadArrayHeader at v2.5.303](https://github.com/MessagePack-CSharp/MessagePack-CSharp/blob/v2.5.303/src/MessagePack.UnityClient/Assets/Scripts/MessagePack/MessagePackReader.cs#L361-L371): it calls `ReserveMinimumChildBytes(count)` before returning. A count exceeding the remaining bytes throws there, before the new array can be allocated.

### Exceptions (if any)

The published input follows the existing parse-error path, reported as `Reading array length for 'streamIds' failed.` It does not reach the claimed count-sized allocation. No new local execution was performed for this adjudication.

### .NET Version

Issues.Title: ASP.NET Core's Web JSON preset keeps AllowDuplicateProperties enabled, and JsonElement has no case-insensitive lookup, so inspect-then-bind diverges
Issues.Body:
### Description

Two measurements about the JSON options ASP.NET Core binds request bodies with, on `10.0.14`. Neither is a new behaviour in isolation, but together they make inspect-then-bind silently inconsistent, and I could not find either written down for ASP.NET Core specifically.

**1. The Web preset keeps `AllowDuplicateProperties = true`.**

```
default : AllowDuplicateProperties=True   PropertyNameCaseInsensitive=False
Web     : AllowDuplicateProperties=True   PropertyNameCaseInsensitive=True
Strict  : AllowDuplicateProperties=False  PropertyNameCaseInsensitive=False
```

`JsonSerializerOptions`' own XML documentation says duplicate property names "can create security vulnerabilities since they introduce ambiguity", and dotnet/runtime#108521 added `AllowDuplicateProperties` so it can be turned off, with `JsonSerializerOptions.Strict` doing so. The `Web` preset that minimal APIs and MVC use does not, so a request body with a repeated property binds without complaint. dotnet/runtime#122181 argued the runtime-wide default; this is about the ASP.NET Core preset, which that issue does not cover.

**2. `JsonElement` has no case-insensitive lookup, while binding is case-insensitive.**

`JsonElement.TryGetProperty` has six overloads and none takes a `StringComparison`; `JsonElement.cs` contains no `StringComparison` or `IgnoreCase` at all, and `JsonObject.TryGetPropertyValue` is the same. So an application that inspects the body before binding cannot use the same matching rules the binder will use.

### What that looks like in practice

A minimal API that reads the raw body first, which is what auditing, request signing and filtering middleware do, and then lets the framework bind:

```csharp
public class Body { public string role { get; set; } }

app.MapPost("/bind", async (HttpContext ctx) =>
{
    ctx.Request.EnableBuffering();
    using var r = new StreamReader(ctx.Request.Body, Encoding.UTF8, leaveOpen: true);
    string raw = await r.ReadToEndAsync();
    ctx.Request.Body.Position = 0;

    using var doc = JsonDocument.Parse(raw);
    string inspected = doc.RootElement.TryGetProperty("role", out var v) ? v.GetString() : "(absent)";

    Body model = await ctx.Request.ReadFromJsonAsync<Body>();

    return Results.Text($"inspected={inspected} bound={model?.role}");
});
```

Measured on `10.0.14`:

| request body | `JsonDocument` sees | the framework binds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `{"role":"user"}` | `user` | `user` |
| `{"Role":"admin"}` | **`(absent)`** | **`admin`** |
| `{"role":"user","Role":"admin"}` | **`user`** | **`admin`** |
| `{"Role":"admin","role":"user"}` | `user` | `user` |
| `{"role":"user","role":"admin"}` | `admin` | `admin` |
| `{"role":"admin","role":"user"}` | `user` | `user` |

The first row is the control: with one ordinary property the two agree, so the disagreement in rows two and three is about the matching rules and not about the reading.

The caller chooses which value each layer sees by choosing the case and the order. Row two is the sharpest: an inspection that asks "is `role` present, and is this value allowed?" finds nothing to check, and the model still receives `admin`.

### What is not divergent, so this is not overstated

For exact duplicates, the last two rows, `JsonDocument` and the binder agree: both take the last occurrence. In-process there is no disagreement on that axis. It matters only when something else in the chain takes the first occurrence, which is where the runtime's "ambiguity" wording comes from and why the two points are worth separating.

### Suggested directions

1. Consider `AllowDuplicateProperties = false` in the Web preset, or say in the ASP.NET Core JSON documentation that it is on and what the consequence is. `Strict` exists but an application that wants only this one behaviour has to rebuild the Web defaults by hand.
2. An overload of `JsonElement.TryGetProperty` taking a `StringComparison`, or a note in the `JsonElement` documentation that it is ordinal while the Web defaults are not, would let inspect-then-bind be written correctly. Right now matching the binder means enumerating the object and reimplementing the last-match tie-break.

Issues.Title: Request Delegate Generator returns HTTP 500 instead of 400 for failed form antiforgery validation (.NET 10 and 11 RC3)
Issues.Body:
### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

I searched open and closed issues for RequestDelegateGenerator/RDG, generated form binding, antiforgery + 500, TryResolveFormAsync, and HandleUncheckedAntiforgeryValidationFeature.

Related: #68054 describes MVC's FormValueProviderFactory encountering this exception and requests a troubleshooting/logging escape hatch and response customization. This report concerns a specific generated minimal API binding defect: the equivalent runtime RequestDelegateFactory already returns 400, while RDG returns 500. #68666 concerns an OpenID Connect callback's form-reading path, not generated minimal API binding. #67588 concerns passkey token/cookie plumbing; #69676 concerns RDG header binding. I did not find an issue tracking this RDG/RDF discrepancy.

### Describe the bug

For a minimal API endpoint with a single `[FromForm] string` parameter, setting `EnableRequestDelegateGenerator=true` changes the response to failed antiforgery validation from HTTP 400 to HTTP 500. The handler is not reached: generated binding throws while checking `HttpRequest.HasFormContentType`.

This reproduces with automatic validation on ASP.NET Core 11 RC3, and with explicit `AddAntiforgery`/`UseAntiforgery` on ASP.NET Core 10.0.14. **It is not a .NET 11-only regression:** SDK 10.0.403 reproduces the same generated-binding failure on 10.0.14.

The repro uses only the Web SDK and a string form-bound endpoint. No RazorSlices, TempData, third-party packages, custom validation feature, token filters, or workaround middleware are involved.

### Expected Behavior

Generated and runtime form binding should both return HTTP 400 when the framework's antiforgery validation feature reports failure, without an unhandled exception or invocation of the form-bound handler. Valid requests should continue to bind normally.

### Steps To Reproduce

Public runnable repro and the complete measured response matrix: https://gist.github.com/DamianEdwards/a6aa48d7aff74b7011b2e0f603f8dfd3 (also cloneable as a public Git repository).

The essential .NET 11 app is:

```xml
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFramework>net11.0</TargetFramework>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
    <EnableRequestDelegateGenerator>true</EnableRequestDelegateGenerator>
  </PropertyGroup>
</Project>
```

```csharp
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc;

var builder = WebApplication.CreateSlimBuilder(args);
var app = builder.Build();
app.MapPost("/form", ([FromForm] string message) => $"handler:{message}");
app.Run();
```

With SDK 11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148 installed, run the app outside the aspnetcore source checkout:

```powershell
dotnet run --project FormRepro.csproj -c Release -- --urls http://127.0.0.1:5181
```

Then send a nonempty, well-formed form body:

```powershell
curl.exe -i http://127.0.0.1:5181/form -H "Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site" -H "Origin: https://attacker.example" -H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" --data "message=hello"
```

Actual: HTTP 500 and the exception below. Change only `EnableRequestDelegateGenerator` to `false`, rebuild/restart, and repeat: HTTP 400. `Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin` with `Origin: http://127.0.0.1:5181` returns HTTP 200 and `handler:hello` in both modes. `Sec-Fetch-Site: same-site` with the mismatched Origin, and an Origin mismatch without Sec-Fetch-Site, also produce 500 with RDG versus 400 without it.

The public repro's Program.cs additionally includes conditional .NET 10 setup (`AddAntiforgery`, `UseAntiforgery`, and a `/token` endpoint that calls `GetAndStoreTokens`). Its PowerShell 7 runner pins each installed SDK by executing that SDK's MSBuild.dll with its matching SDK directory, removes inherited SDK overrides from build subprocesses, isolates build/generated output for every variant, starts real Kestrel processes in Production, sends requests using HttpClient, checks every response, and stops its own servers. It saves generated sources, build logs, server exception logs, runtime host traces, and results.json under `evidence`.

Measured results (all 24 requests checked):

| SDK | Target / loaded ASP.NET Core runtime | Requests rejected by validation | RDG enabled | RDG disabled | Valid control, both modes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148 | net11.0 / 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148 | cross-site; same-site with mismatched Origin; mismatched Origin fallback | 500 each | 400 each | 200, handler:hello |
| 11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148 | net10.0 / 10.0.14 | missing token; invalid token; valid token without matching cookie | 500 each | 400 each | 200, handler:hello |
| 10.0.403 | net10.0 / 10.0.14 | missing token; invalid token; valid token without matching cookie | 500 each | 400 each | 200, handler:hello |

Run the complete matrix on Windows with those SDKs installed:

```powershell
git clone https://gist.github.com/a6aa48d7aff74b7011b2e0f603f8dfd3.git form-repro
pwsh -File .\form-repro\Run-Repro.ps1
```

### Exceptions (if any)

ASP.NET Core 11 RC3 (generated names abbreviated and local paths omitted):

```text
System.InvalidOperationException: This form is being accessed with a failed antiforgery validation. Validate the `IAntiforgeryValidationFeature` on the request before reading from the form.
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http.Features.FormFeature.HandleUncheckedAntiforgeryValidationFeature()
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http.Features.FormFeature.get_HasFormContentType()
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http.Generated.GeneratedRouteBuilderExtensionsCore.TryResolveFormAsync(...) in GeneratedRouteBuilderExtensions.g.cs:line 363
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http.Generated.GeneratedRouteBuilderExtensionsCore...MapPost1...RequestHandler... in GeneratedRouteBuilderExtensions.g.cs:line 204
```

ASP.NET Core 10.0.14 has the same call path; its message starts `This form is being accessed with an invalid anti-forgery token.`

### .NET Version

11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148 and 10.0.403 (separately pinned build SDKs).

### Anything else?

- OS: Windows; Release builds, `WebApplication.CreateSlimBuilder`, Production environment, loopback HTTP, no IDE required.
- Runtime host traces confirm that the actual loaded shared frameworks are Microsoft.NETCore.App and Microsoft.AspNetCore.App 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148 for net11.0, and 10.0.14 for net10.0.
- Diagnostic compiler invocations identify the RDG analyzer from `Microsoft.AspNetCore.App.Ref/11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148` for net11.0 and `Microsoft.AspNetCore.App.Ref/10.0.14` for net10.0 under **both** SDKs. The generator comes from the target's reference pack, so the net10.0 build under SDK 11 is not evidence that it uses the .NET 11 generator.
- RDG-enabled variants emitted `GeneratedRouteBuilderExtensions.g.cs` with interception attributes and the form helper, and failed requests' stacks name that generated handler. RDG-disabled variants emitted no RDG source. This is an actual generated/runtime comparison, not just an unverified property toggle.
- In the emitted helper, `TryResolveFormAsync` checks body presence and then reads `HasFormContentType` without checking `IAntiforgeryValidationFeature.IsValid`. Its catch clauses handle BadHttpRequestException, IOException, and InvalidDataException, not this InvalidOperationException; moreover, the throwing property access precedes the try block.
- The runtime RequestDelegateFactory's form-binding helper checks `IAntiforgeryValidationFeature` for `IsValid: false` before accessing `HasFormContentType`, and sets status 400.
- The same missing check remains in the current main source inspected at commit `4f556f73a610b386e5ec29355a300e493d30c4c5`: [generated helper source](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/4f556f73a610b386e5ec29355a300e493d30c4c5/src/Http/Http.Extensions/gen/Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http.RequestDelegateGenerator/RequestDelegateGeneratorSources.cs), [runtime binding source](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/4f556f73a610b386e5ec29355a300e493d30c4c5/src/Http/Http.Extensions/src/RequestDelegateFactory.cs). Current main was inspected, not built; executable measurements above use the identified installed releases.

Issues.Title: Use span-based data protection in SecureDataFormat
Issues.Body:
# Use span-based data protection in SecureDataFormat

- [x] You've read the [Contributor Guide](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CODE-OF-CONDUCT.md).
- [x] You've included unit or integration tests for your change, where applicable.
- [x] You've included inline docs for your change, where applicable.
- [ ] There's an open issue for the PR that you are making. If you'd like to propose a new feature or change, please open an issue to discuss the change or find an existing issue.

Cut allocations by 14–15% for ticket `Unprotect` and by 24–26% for `Protect`. Every cookie-authenticated request runs `Unprotect`.

## Description

`SecureDataFormat<T>` (used by `TicketDataFormat`, which backs cookie auth, and by `PropertiesDataFormat` for remote auth state) allocates two full-size intermediate arrays on every call:
- `Unprotect` base64url-decodes the cookie into a new `byte[]`, then calls `IDataProtector.Unprotect(byte[])`.
- `Protect` gets a new protected `byte[]` from `IDataProtector.Protect`, then base64url-encodes it.

The default data protector already implements `ISpanDataProtector`, which Antiforgery and `CookieTempDataProvider` already use. This PR uses it in `SecureDataFormat` too:
- **Unprotect:** decode with `Base64Url.DecodeFromChars` into a pooled buffer and decrypt into a pooled `RefPooledArrayBufferWriter`. Then copy the plaintext out once, because `IDataSerializer<T>.Deserialize` takes a `byte[]`. If the text isn't strict base64url (`Base64UrlTextEncoder.Decode` also accepts standard base64 with `+`/`/`), it falls back to the existing array path, so accepted inputs and results don't change.
- **Protect:** encrypt into a pooled writer and base64url-encode straight from the written span.
- Protectors that don't implement `ISpanDataProtector` keep the existing code path.
- The pooled buffers stay local to the call and never reach callers. Buffers that may hold plaintext are cleared before they go back to the pool.

No public API or behavior change. Exceptions are still swallowed and `Unprotect` still returns `default`.

### Benchmarks

Local BenchmarkDotNet (in-process, Release, 2 vCPU Linux). Each cell shows 3 interleaved base/PR rounds. `SecureDataFormatBenchmark` (ticket shaped like an Identity cookie) and `CookieAuthenticationBenchmark` (full `HttpContext.AuthenticateAsync` with cookie auth, including DI scope and context) are added in this PR.

| Benchmark | main (ns) | PR (ns) | Δ time | main alloc | PR alloc | Δ alloc |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Unprotect, 7 claims | 7,862 / 7,865 / 7,921 | 7,814 / 7,756 / 7,801 | −1.2% | 5,744 B | 4,944 B | **−14%** |
| Unprotect, 100 claims | 27,608 / 28,494 / 28,465 | 26,797 / 27,581 / 27,160 | −3.6% | 53,699 B | 45,554 B | **−15%** |
| Protect, 7 claims | 10,515 / 10,547 / 10,740 | 10,356 / 10,400 / 10,310 | −2.3% | 7,304 B | 5,544 B | **−24%** |
| Protect, 100 claims | 34,062 / 35,029 / 34,247 | 32,648 / 33,320 / 32,860 | −4.4% | 63,331 B | 46,882 B | **−26%** |
| Cookie AuthenticateAsync | 11,022 / 10,731 / 11,053 | 10,918 / 10,773 / 10,549 | −1.7% | 12,873 B | 11,961 B | **−7%** |
| Cookie AuthenticateAsync, chunked cookie | 36,638 / 35,676 / 37,314 | 35,756 / 35,215 / 35,342 | −3.0% | 94,764 B | 87,660 B | **−7.5%** |
| Cookie AuthenticateAsync, no cookie (control) | 884 / 849 / 858 | 838 / 868 / 845 | ~0 | 2,424 B | 2,424 B | 0 |

This change is independent of #70165 and #70172 (ticket deserialization and serialization), and their savings add to these.

### Tests

`Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.Test`: 726 passed, 3 skipped (pre-existing skips). New `SecureDataFormatTests`:
- The default protector (and a purpose-derived one) takes the span path.
- Span and array protectors interoperate in both directions, with and without a purpose, for payloads from 0 B to 100 KB (larger than the initial pooled buffers).
- Standard base64 input (with `+`/`/`) still unprotects through the fallback.
- Invalid input (empty, bad length, invalid characters, mixed base64/base64url, wrong ciphertext) returns null on both paths.

**🤖 Posted by ASP.NET Core Perf 2 (AI Agent)**


### Update: review feedback (6a382bbaf0)

Replaced `RefPooledArrayBufferWriter`, whose `GetMemory` throws, with a private pooled struct writer that supports both `GetSpan` and `GetMemory`. Custom `ISpanDataProtector` implementations that write through `GetMemory` now work. Added the `SpanProtectorsUsingGetMemoryAreSupported` tests: they fail without the fix and pass with it. The full Authentication tests pass: 730 passed, 3 skipped.

Re-measured base vs. updated PR (Release, BenchmarkDotNet in-process, 3 interleaved rounds, mean of rounds):

| Benchmark | Base | PR | Δ time | Allocated (base → PR) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Protect (7 claims) | 10.54 µs | 10.47 µs | −0.6% | 7,304 B → 5,544 B (−24%) |
| Unprotect (7 claims) | 7.88 µs | 7.93 µs | +0.6% | 5,744 B → 4,944 B (−14%) |
| Protect (100 claims) | 34.70 µs | 33.42 µs | −3.7% | 63,331 B → 46,882 B (−26%) |

| Cookie AuthenticateAsync | 10.83 µs | 10.69 µs | −1.3% | 12,873 B → 11,961 B (−7%) |
| Cookie AuthenticateAsync (chunked) | 35.97 µs | 35.92 µs | −0.1% | 94,764 B → 87,660 B (−7.5%) |
| No cookie (control) | 852 ns | 847 ns | −0.6% | 2,424 B → 2,424 B |

Issues.Title: Speed up Base32.FromBase32 decoding for authenticator keys
Issues.Body:
## Summary

`Base32.FromBase32` decodes the authenticator key on every `AuthenticatorTokenProvider.ValidateAsync` call, which is authenticator-app 2FA.

The current decoder has two costs:
- Per character, it does a `string.IndexOf(char.ToUpperInvariant(c))` over the 32-char alphabet.
- Its loop moves only 1–5 bits per iteration. For a 32-char key that's about 52 iterations, each with a read-modify-write of `output[outputIndex]`.

This PR:
- Maps `A-Z`, `a-z` and `2-7` with three range checks. Other ASCII characters return invalid. **Non-ASCII characters still use the original `IndexOf(char.ToUpperInvariant(c))` lookup**, so culture-invariant casing quirks are unchanged.
- Uses a standard 5-bit accumulator that emits a byte whenever at least 8 bits are buffered.

What stays the same:
- The loop still stops when the output buffer is full. It consumes and validates exactly the same characters as before, so trailing unused characters are still not validated.
- Output bytes and `FormatException` behavior are identical.
- The encoding side, `GenerateBase32` and `ToBase32`, is untouched.
- No public API changes.

Equivalence check, run outside the repo: old and new decoders compared on 2,000,000 random strings of length 0–39. Inputs were drawn from valid characters, lowercase, `=`, digits 0/1/8/9, space and assorted non-ASCII characters. The check also covered all 65,536 `char` values as an 8-char string. Bytes and exception types matched in every case.

## Benchmarks

Real `Base32.FromBase32` in Release builds of `Microsoft.Extensions.Identity.Core` (main vs. PR), net12.0, BenchmarkDotNet with MemoryDiagnoser. The two builds ran interleaved over 3 rounds. The input is a key from `Base32.GenerateBase32()` (32 chars, the default authenticator key).

| Method | main (R1 / R2 / R3) | PR (R1 / R2 / R3) | Allocated |
|---|---|---|---|
| FromBase32 (uppercase key) | 230.1 / 225.9 / 229.9 ns | **48.8 / 49.5 / 49.2 ns** | 48 B → 48 B |
| FromBase32 (lowercase key) | 236.5 / 240.0 / 236.7 ns | **61.7 / 57.2 / 57.6 ns** | 48 B → 48 B |

Decoding is about **4.6× faster** and saves ~180 ns per authenticator validation. That's roughly 5% of the HMAC window cost once #70226 lands.

## Tests

- New `Base32Test` cases:
  - RFC 4648 test vectors (`f` … `foobar`), with and without padding.
  - Lowercase input, all-zero and all-one groups, and inputs too short to produce a byte.
  - Unconsumed trailing characters, which are still not validated (`"MZ!"`).
  - `FormatException` for invalid ASCII just outside each range (`@ [ \` { 0 1 8`), for `!`, space, `=` in the middle, and non-ASCII (`é`, Kelvin sign, fullwidth `Ａ`).
- These new tests pass on both main and this PR.
- `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Identity.Test`: 591 passed, 0 failed, 1 skipped. `IdentityUIScriptsTest` was excluded because it needs CDN network access.
- `Microsoft.Extensions.Identity.Core` builds for net12.0, netstandard2.0 and net462.

Issues.Title: Speed up TOTP validation by reusing the HMAC and input buffer across timesteps
Issues.Body:
## Summary

`Rfc6238AuthenticationService` is used by every TOTP-based token provider:
- `TotpSecurityStampBasedTokenProvider`, `EmailTokenProvider` and `PhoneNumberTokenProvider`, which handle 2FA, email/phone confirmation and change-email/phone codes;
- `AuthenticatorTokenProvider`, which handles authenticator-app 2FA.

Validation checks up to 5 timesteps (±2). On .NET 6+, each check paid for:
1. **Re-keying HMAC-SHA1 for every timestep.** The one-shot `HMACSHA1.TryHashData(key, …)` sets up a new HMAC context with the same key 5 times.
2. **Re-encoding the modifier and building a new `[timestep][modifier]` array for every timestep.** These are `_encoding.GetBytes(modifier)` plus `ApplyModifier`.

This PR:
- Adds `ValidateCodeInWindow`, which creates **one** `IncrementalHash` HMAC-SHA1 per validation and reuses it for every timestep via `AppendData` and `TryGetHashAndReset`. `ValidateCode` and `AuthenticatorTokenProvider.ValidateAsync` both use it. The netstandard2.0/net462 path already reuses a single `HMACSHA1` instance in the same way.
- Encodes the modifier once into a `[8-byte timestep][UTF-8 modifier]` buffer and rewrites only the timestep (`BinaryPrimitives.WriteUInt64BigEndian`) per HMAC. `GenerateCode` uses the same buffer.
- Writes the HMAC output into a small buffer that is zeroed in `finally` with `CryptographicOperations.ZeroMemory`.
- `IncrementalHash.CreateHMAC(ReadOnlySpan)` keeps no managed key copy on Unix (`blockSize == -1`). The CNG provider's copy is cleared on `Dispose`, which runs through `using`.

What stays the same:
- The HMAC input bytes: the same big-endian timestep and the same strict-UTF-8 modifier bytes. Generated and accepted codes are identical.
- The window (±2), the time sources, and the casting semantics. Callers keep using `(ulong)(timestep + i)`.
- `ComputeTotp(byte[], ulong, byte[]?)` keeps its signature. Identity.FunctionalTests link-compiles this file and uses it.
- The netstandard2.0/net462 code path.
- No public API changes.

## Benchmarks

Calls the real `Rfc6238AuthenticationService` in Release builds of `Microsoft.Extensions.Identity.Core` (main vs. PR), net12.0, BenchmarkDotNet with MemoryDiagnoser. The two builds ran interleaved over 3 rounds. The modifier is `"Totp:TwoFactor:" + Guid`, as used by `TotpSecurityStampBasedTokenProvider`. The `NoModifier` case is the same code path `AuthenticatorTokenProvider` now uses.

| Method | main (R1 / R2 / R3) | PR (R1 / R2 / R3) | Alloc main → PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| GenerateCode | 1.294 / 1.286 / 1.281 µs | 1.241 / 1.264 / 1.240 µs | 168 B → **88 B** |
| ValidateCode, match (3rd timestep) | 3.630 / 3.745 / 3.717 µs | **2.925 / 2.945 / 2.911 µs** | 344 B → 352 B |
| ValidateCode, no match (5 HMACs) | 6.117 / 6.150 / 6.101 µs | **3.980 / 4.036 / 3.998 µs** | 520 B → **352 B** |
| ValidateCode, no match, no modifier | 5.688 / 5.827 / 5.776 µs | **3.771 / 3.850 / 3.778 µs** | 0 B → 296 B |

- Validation is about **21% faster** when the code matches and about **35% faster** when it doesn't, which is the worst case and the one hit by brute-force attempts.
- Allocations drop for modifier-based providers.
- The authenticator / no-modifier path now allocates ~300 B for the `IncrementalHash` and buffers, in exchange for ~2 µs less CPU per validation.

## Tests

- New `Rfc6238AuthenticationServiceTest` (16 cases):
  - `GenerateCode` and `ValidateCode` match the reference `ComputeTotp(key, timestep, UTF8(modifier))` for a null modifier, an empty one, an ASCII one and a non-ASCII/surrogate-pair one.
  - `ValidateCodeInWindow` agrees with a reference ±2 loop built on `ComputeTotp` for in-window, out-of-window (±3, ±4) and garbage codes. The keys cover lengths 0, 10, 20, 64 and 100, including longer than the HMAC block size.
  - `AuthenticatorTokenProvider.ValidateAsync` accepts codes within the window and rejects non-numeric tokens.
- `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Identity.Test`: 581 passed, 0 failed, 1 skipped. `IdentityUIScriptsTest` was excluded because it needs CDN network access.
- `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Identity.InMemory.Test`: 226 passed.
- `Microsoft.Extensions.Identity.Core` builds for net12.0, netstandard2.0 and net462.

# Avoid an extra task allocation in DefaultAuthorizationServiceImpl.AuthorizeAsync

- [x] You've read the [Contributor Guide](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CODE-OF-CONDUCT.md).
- [x] You've included unit or integration tests for your change, where applicable.
- [x] You've included inline docs for your change, where applicable.
- [ ] There's an open issue for the PR that you are making. (Perf finding, no separate issue.)

Save 72 B per authorization check when handlers complete synchronously.

## Description

### Problem
`DefaultAuthorizationServiceImpl` is the `IAuthorizationService` registered by `AddAuthorizationCore()`. It wraps `DefaultAuthorizationService.AuthorizeAsync(user, resource, requirements)` in an `async` method so it can record the `aspnetcore.authorization.attempts` metric. That overload is the one used by `PolicyEvaluator` (and therefore `AuthorizationMiddleware`), MVC's `AuthorizeFilter` and the `AuthorizeAsync(user, resource, policy)` extension. Because the wrapper is an `async` method, it allocates a second `Task<AuthorizationResult>` on top of the base method's task on **every** authorization check. That happens even when the result is already available, which is the normal case because built-in and most custom handlers complete synchronously.

### Change
- Call the base method. If its task has already run to completion, record the metric with its result and return **the same task**.
- Otherwise, including faulted, canceled or still-pending tasks, go through the original `try`/`await`/`catch` logic in a helper `async` method. That path still records the result, or the exception, and rethrows exactly as before.

`DefaultAuthorizationService.AuthorizeAsync` is an `async` method, so it never throws synchronously. Exceptions keep surfacing through the returned task, and metrics are still recorded exactly once per call with the same tags. The base class (`DefaultAuthorizationService.cs`) is untouched. `TaskStatus.RanToCompletion` is used instead of `IsCompletedSuccessfully` to keep the netstandard2.0 and net462 builds working. There are no public API changes.

### Benchmarks
New `DefaultAuthorizationServiceBenchmark`: `AddAuthorizationCore()` and `AuthorizeAsync(user, null, policy)`. BenchmarkDotNet with `[MemoryDiagnoser]`, in-process, 3 warmup and 15 measured iterations, 3 interleaved A/B rounds:

| Round | Benchmark | main | PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | RequireAuthenticatedUser | 284.1 ns, 632 B | 241.6 ns, 560 B |
| 1 | RequireRole | 302.5 ns, 704 B | 282.7 ns, 632 B |
| 2 | RequireAuthenticatedUser | 241.7 ns, 632 B | 255.2 ns, 560 B |
| 2 | RequireRole | 303.4 ns, 704 B | 287.2 ns, 632 B |
| 3 | RequireAuthenticatedUser | 249.3 ns, 632 B | 239.3 ns, 560 B |
| 3 | RequireRole | 304.0 ns, 704 B | 273.2 ns, 632 B |

The result is **72 B (about 11%) less allocated per authorization check**, consistent across every round. Time improves by about 5–10% in most rounds; `RequireAuthenticatedUser` in round 2 was within noise.

### Tests
- The existing `AuthorizationMetricsTest` cases cover synchronous success, failure and handler exceptions.
- New: `Authorize_WithoutPolicyName_AsyncHandler` (success and failure) and `Authorize_WithoutPolicyName_ExceptionThrownInAsyncHandler`. These cover the asynchronous path and check that the metric is recorded only after completion, with the right result or `error.type`.
- New: `Authorize_WithoutPolicyName_MetricsListenerThrows_ExceptionSurfacesThroughTask`. It covers the faulted and canceled cases and checks that a throwing measurement listener surfaces through the returned task rather than synchronously.
- `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authorization.Test`: **172 passed, 0 failed** (net12.0). `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authorization` builds for net462, netstandard2.0 and net12.0 with no warnings.

# Reduce per-call overhead in UserValidator

- [x] You've read the [Contributor Guide](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CODE-OF-CONDUCT.md).
- [x] You've included unit or integration tests for your change, where applicable.
- [x] You've included inline docs for your change, where applicable.
- [ ] There's an open issue for the PR that you are making. If you'd like to propose a new feature or change, please open an issue to discuss the change or find an existing issue.

Check allowed user name characters with cached `SearchValues` and reuse one `EmailAddressAttribute`.

## Description

`UserValidator<TUser>.ValidateAsync` runs on every `CreateAsync`/`UpdateAsync` and on user name and email changes. It had two avoidable costs:

1. **Allowed characters check.** The check was `userName.Any(c => !manager.Options.User.AllowedUserNameCharacters.Contains(c))`. This allocates a closure and delegate per call. It also re-reads the options and does a linear `string.Contains` over the 65-character default set for every character of the user name.
2. **Email format check.** `new EmailAddressAttribute()` was constructed on every call when `RequireUniqueEmail` is enabled. The attribute's constructor does a resource lookup for its default error message.

**Change:**
- On .NET 8+, the allowed-characters check uses `ContainsAnyExcept(SearchValues<char>)`. The `SearchValues` is cached in a static field, keyed by the configured `AllowedUserNameCharacters` string with an ordinal comparison. If the option changes, the cache is rebuilt, and a new test covers this. The cache is static because `UserValidator` is registered as scoped. It only holds data derived from configuration, never user input, and isn't reachable by callers. On netstandard2.0/net462, a plain loop with `string.IndexOf(char)` replaces the LINQ closure.
- The `EmailAddressAttribute` is now a `static readonly` instance. `EmailAddressAttribute.IsValid` is stateless.
- No public API or behavior changes. Matching is still ordinal per UTF-16 code unit, and null/empty `AllowedUserNameCharacters` still disables the check.

### Benchmark

Interleaved A/B on the same machine, 3 rounds. Each round runs `main` then this PR, using Release builds of `Microsoft.Extensions.Identity.Core` (net12.0) and BenchmarkDotNet's in-process toolchain. The benchmark calls the real `UserValidator<TUser>.ValidateAsync` with a `UserManager` over a no-op store whose `FindByName`/`FindByEmail` return null. The user name/email is `someone.longer@example.com`.

| Method | Round | main Mean | PR Mean | main Alloc | PR Alloc |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Validate_Default | 1 | 142.8 ns | 83.05 ns | 320 B | 296 B |
| Validate_Default | 2 | 144.0 ns | 85.00 ns | 320 B | 296 B |
| Validate_Default | 3 | 145.7 ns | 83.49 ns | 320 B | 296 B |
| Validate_RequireUniqueEmail | 1 | 277.3 ns | 166.52 ns | 544 B | 520 B |
| Validate_RequireUniqueEmail | 2 | 282.5 ns | 167.33 ns | 544 B | 520 B |
| Validate_RequireUniqueEmail | 3 | 278.1 ns | 168.40 ns | 544 B | 520 B |

That's about −42% time with default options and −40% with `RequireUniqueEmail`. Most of the remaining time and allocation is the async state machine and store calls.

In isolation on .NET 10, the allowed-characters check for this user name drops from 52.7 ns to 2.5 ns. Constructing and running `EmailAddressAttribute` drops from 60 ns / 88 B to 6.7 ns / 0 B. I also measured an uncached `IndexOfAnyExcept(string)`: it was *slower* than `main` (79 ns) because it rebuilds a probabilistic map for the 65-character set on every call, which is why the `SearchValues` is cached.

<details><summary>Benchmark code</summary>

```csharp
[MemoryDiagnoser]
public class UserValidatorBench
{
    readonly UserValidator<TestUser> _v = new();
    readonly UserManager<TestUser> _default = Mgr.Create(_ => { });
    readonly UserManager<TestUser> _uniqueEmail = Mgr.Create(o => o.User.RequireUniqueEmail = true);
    readonly TestUser _user = new(); // UserName = Email = "someone.longer@example.com"

    [Benchmark] public Task<IdentityResult> Validate_Default() => _v.ValidateAsync(_default, _user);
    [Benchmark] public Task<IdentityResult> Validate_RequireUniqueEmail() => _v.ValidateAsync(_uniqueEmail, _user);
}

static class Mgr
{
    public static UserManager<TestUser> Create(Action<IdentityOptions> configure)
    {
        var o = new IdentityOptions(); configure(o);
        return new UserManager<TestUser>(new NoopStore(), Options.Create(o), null!, null!, null!,
            new UpperInvariantLookupNormalizer(), null!, null!, NullLogger<UserManager<TestUser>>.Instance);
    }
}
```
</details>

### Tests

- New `UsesCurrentAllowedUserNameCharacters` test. It changes `AllowedUserNameCharacters` between calls on the same validator, including non-ASCII characters, and checks that the current value is always honored.
- `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Identity.Test`: 566 passed, 0 failed, 1 skipped. The 16 `IdentityUIScriptsTest` CDN tests were excluded locally because they need network access the sandbox does not have.
- `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Identity.InMemory.Test` (user manager specification tests): 226/226 passed.
- `Microsoft.Extensions.Identity.Core` builds cleanly for net12.0, netstandard2.0 and net462.

# Avoid LINQ and allocations in PasswordValidator

- [x] You've read the [Contributor Guide](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CODE-OF-CONDUCT.md).
- [x] You've included unit or integration tests for your change, where applicable.
- [x] You've included inline docs for your change, where applicable.
- [ ] There's an open issue for the PR that you are making. If you'd like to propose a new feature or change, please open an issue to discuss the change or find an existing issue.

Validate passwords without LINQ delegates, enumerators or a `HashSet<char>`.

## Description

`PasswordValidator<TUser>.ValidateAsync` runs on every user creation, password change and password reset. It used LINQ over the password string:

- `password.All(IsLetterOrDigit)` and `password.Any(IsDigit/IsLower/IsUpper)`. Each call allocates a delegate bound to the virtual instance method and a string enumerator.
- `password.Distinct().Count()`. This allocates a `HashSet<char>` plus the iterator and always walks the whole password, even when `RequiredUniqueChars` is 1, which is the default.

**Change:**
- Replace `All`/`Any` with private `foreach` helpers that call the same virtual `IsLetterOrDigit`/`IsDigit`/`IsLower`/`IsUpper` methods, in the same order and with the same short-circuiting. Overrides still apply.
- Replace `Distinct().Count() < RequiredUniqueChars` with `HasMinimumUniqueChars`. It tracks ASCII characters in two `ulong` bitmaps, falls back to a lazily created `HashSet<char>` only for non-ASCII characters, and returns as soon as `RequiredUniqueChars` distinct characters have been seen. Distinctness is still ordinal per UTF-16 code unit, the same as `Enumerable.Distinct` on `char`.
- No public API or behavior changes. Errors, their order and the result are unchanged.

### Benchmark

Interleaved A/B on the same machine, 3 rounds. Each round runs `main` then this PR, using Release builds of `Microsoft.Extensions.Identity.Core` (net12.0) and BenchmarkDotNet's in-process toolchain. Each benchmark calls the real `PasswordValidator<TUser>.ValidateAsync` with a `UserManager` backed by a no-op store.

| Method | Round | main Mean | PR Mean | main Alloc | PR Alloc |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Validate_Default | 1 | 233.6 ns | 16.84 ns | 832 B | 72 B |
| Validate_Default | 2 | 247.8 ns | 16.72 ns | 832 B | 72 B |
| Validate_Default | 3 | 245.9 ns | 17.07 ns | 832 B | 72 B |
| Validate_RequiredUniqueChars6 | 1 | 236.4 ns | 23.50 ns | 832 B | 72 B |
| Validate_RequiredUniqueChars6 | 2 | 240.6 ns | 23.74 ns | 832 B | 72 B |
| Validate_RequiredUniqueChars6 | 3 | 243.5 ns | 23.35 ns | 832 B | 72 B |
| Validate_Weak (fails all checks) | 1 | 576.5 ns | 445.83 ns | 1,080 B | 816 B |
| Validate_Weak (fails all checks) | 2 | 517.7 ns | 447.92 ns | 1,080 B | 816 B |
| Validate_Weak (fails all checks) | 3 | 528.4 ns | 458.92 ns | 1,080 B | 816 B |

For a valid password, validation is about 14x faster (−93%) and allocates 760 B less. The remaining 72 B is the returned `Task<IdentityResult>`. The failing case is dominated by building the `IdentityError` messages, but still saves 264 B and about 14%.

<details><summary>Benchmark code</summary>

```csharp
[MemoryDiagnoser]
public class PasswordValidatorBench
{
    readonly PasswordValidator<TestUser> _v = new();
    readonly UserManager<TestUser> _default = Mgr.Create(_ => { });
    readonly UserManager<TestUser> _unique = Mgr.Create(o => o.Password.RequiredUniqueChars = 6);
    readonly TestUser _user = new();

    [Benchmark] public Task<IdentityResult> Validate_Default() => _v.ValidateAsync(_default, _user, "P@ssw0rd!Secure123");
    [Benchmark] public Task<IdentityResult> Validate_RequiredUniqueChars6() => _v.ValidateAsync(_unique, _user, "P@ssw0rd!Secure123");
    [Benchmark] public Task<IdentityResult> Validate_Weak() => _v.ValidateAsync(_unique, _user, "aaaa");
}

static class Mgr
{
    public static UserManager<TestUser> Create(Action<IdentityOptions> configure)
    {
        var o = new IdentityOptions(); configure(o);
        return new UserManager<TestUser>(new NoopStore(), Options.Create(o), null!, null!, null!,
            new UpperInvariantLookupNormalizer(), null!, null!, NullLogger<UserManager<TestUser>>.Instance);
    }
}
```
</details>

### Tests

- New `PasswordValidatorTest` cases for `RequiredUniqueChars` cover characters at the bitmap boundaries (`'?'`/`'@'`, `'\u007f'`/`'\u0080'`), non-ASCII characters, surrogate pairs and repeated non-ASCII characters.
- `HasMinimumUniqueChars` was also fuzzed locally against `password.Distinct().Count() >= n` on 200,000 random strings (ASCII, Latin-1, CJK, surrogates, boundary chars), with no mismatches.
- `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Identity.Test`: 571 passed, 0 failed, 1 skipped. The 16 `IdentityUIScriptsTest` CDN tests were excluded locally because they need network access the sandbox does not have.

- [x] You've read the [Contributor Guide](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CODE-OF-CONDUCT.md).

Make `UserManager<TUser>` cheaper to construct. It's scoped and gets constructed on every request that resolves `SignInManager`/`ISecurityStampValidator`, which includes every cookie-authenticated request through `SecurityStampValidator.ValidatePrincipalAsync`.

## Description

- The injected `UserValidators` and `PasswordValidators` are added with one `AddRange` into lists whose capacity is set to the collection count, which is known when DI injects an array. Before, a `foreach` over `IEnumerable<T>` boxed an enumerator and grew each list to the default capacity of 4 through `Add`. The lists are still created by field initializers, so they exist before the constructor's virtual `Logger` setter runs.
- The token `ProviderMap` is enumerated once as key/value pairs. Before, the code enumerated `Keys` and then looked each key up with the indexer.

There is no behavior change. Validator order, contents, mutability (`IList<T>` backed by `List<T>`), the null-collection handling and token provider registration order are all unchanged. There are no public API changes.

### Benchmark

Local BenchmarkDotNet run (MemoryDiagnoser, in-process). The baseline and PR builds of `Microsoft.Extensions.Identity.Core.dll` ran in separate shared-framework copies, interleaved A, B, A, B over 3 rounds. The benchmark resolves the service in a new DI scope with `AddIdentityCore<User>().AddSignInManager().AddDefaultTokenProviders()`, a no-op store and `AddLogging()`.

| Method | Round | main Mean | PR Mean | main Alloc | PR Alloc |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Resolve `UserManager<TUser>` | 1 | 1.780 us | 1.667 us | 4.23 KB | 4.13 KB |
| Resolve `UserManager<TUser>` | 2 | 1.781 us | 1.694 us | 4.23 KB | 4.13 KB |
| Resolve `UserManager<TUser>` | 3 | 1.803 us | 1.782 us | 4.23 KB | 4.13 KB |
| Resolve `ISecurityStampValidator` | 1 | 2.911 us | 2.855 us | 5.68 KB | 5.57 KB |
| Resolve `ISecurityStampValidator` | 2 | 2.876 us | 2.887 us | 5.68 KB | 5.57 KB |
| Resolve `ISecurityStampValidator` | 3 | 2.834 us | 2.857 us | 5.68 KB | 5.57 KB |

Every resolve that constructs a `UserManager` allocates about 104 B less. `UserManager` resolve time was about 5% lower in two rounds and about 1% lower in the third. The `ISecurityStampValidator` resolve times are within noise; only its allocation goes down. In an isolated benchmark of the token provider loop with 4 default providers, the loop alone took 56.1 ns on main and 34.5 ns with this PR.

This complements #70174, which caches the metrics objects, and #70175, which caches the logger. Those PRs touch different lines, and this one does not overlap them.

### Tests

I added `UserManagerTest.ConstructorCopiesValidatorsInOrderAndCollectionsAreAvailableToVirtualMembers`, which covers validator order, mutability, null inputs and a derived `Logger` setter that reads the collections. With the final commit, the UserManager, SignInManager, SecurityStamp and claims factory tests pass: 208 passed, 1 skipped. On the first commit, the full `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Identity.Test` run had 565 passed and 1 skipped. The 16 failures were all `IdentityUIScriptsTest` CDN tests (`*_Matches_CDNContent`, `*_SubresourceIntegrityCheck`), which need outbound internet access that isn't available in the environment where I ran them. They don't involve this change.

# Avoid ClaimsPrincipal.Claims iterator allocations in ClaimsAuthorizationRequirement

- [x] You've read the [Contributor Guide](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CODE-OF-CONDUCT.md).

Make `RequireClaim(...)` evaluation about 35% faster with fewer allocations.

## Description

### Problem
`ClaimsAuthorizationRequirement.HandleRequirementAsync` runs for every `RequireClaim(...)` policy check, so it runs on every request to such endpoints. It enumerates `context.User.Claims`. `ClaimsPrincipal.Claims` is a compiler-generated iterator that flattens `Identities` and each identity's `Claims`. Enumerating it allocates the outer iterator plus the nested `Identities` and per-identity enumerators, about 136 B per check, and adds two levels of interface dispatch per claim.

### Change
- If `context.User` is **exactly** `ClaimsPrincipal`, so `Claims` and `Identities` aren't overridden, enumerate `user.Identities` and then each `identity.Claims` directly. That is the same sequence `ClaimsPrincipal.Claims` produces. `identity.Claims` is still called virtually, so derived `ClaimsIdentity` types behave as before.
- Derived `ClaimsPrincipal` types keep using the virtual `Claims` property exactly as before.
- `IList<T>` sources are indexed rather than enumerated.
- The match predicate is unchanged: claim type `OrdinalIgnoreCase`, and if values were specified, value `Ordinal` via `AllowedValues.Contains(value, StringComparer.Ordinal)`. The first match still short-circuits.

There are no public API or behavior changes, and nothing is cached. The project still builds for net462, netstandard2.0 and net12.0.

### Benchmarks
New `ClaimsAuthorizationRequirementBenchmark`: `IAuthorizationService.AuthorizeAsync` with a principal carrying 16 claims, comparing `RequireClaim("permission", "admin", "write")` with `RequireClaim("permission")`. BenchmarkDotNet with `[MemoryDiagnoser]`, in-process, 3 warmup and 15 measured iterations, 3 interleaved A/B rounds:

| Round | Benchmark | main | PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | RequireClaimWithValues | 472.7 ns, 768 B | 292.9 ns, 632 B |
| 1 | RequireClaim | 509.7 ns, 768 B | 289.9 ns, 632 B |
| 2 | RequireClaimWithValues | 467.3 ns, 768 B | 319.9 ns, 632 B |
| 2 | RequireClaim | 494.0 ns, 768 B | 304.1 ns, 632 B |
| 3 | RequireClaimWithValues | 446.1 ns, 768 B | 302.8 ns, 632 B |
| 3 | RequireClaim | 481.1 ns, 768 B | 295.6 ns, 632 B |

That's **about 35–40% faster and 136 B (18%) less allocated per authorization check**. The remaining allocations come from `AuthorizationHandlerContext`, the result and the handler pipeline, which this PR doesn't touch.

### Tests
New tests in `DefaultAuthorizationServiceTests`:
- `Authorize_RequireClaim_SearchesAllIdentities`: the match is in the third identity, with an empty identity in between. Covers case-insensitive type matching and case-sensitive value matching.
- `Authorize_RequireClaimWithNoValues_SearchesAllIdentities`
- `Authorize_RequireClaim_UsesOverriddenPrincipalClaims`: a derived `ClaimsPrincipal` overriding `Claims` is still honored.
- `Authorize_RequireClaim_UsesOverriddenIdentityClaims`: a derived `ClaimsIdentity` overriding `Claims` is still honored.

`Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authorization.Test`: **175 passed, 0 failed** (net12.0).

# Cache the absence of authorization metadata in AuthorizationMiddleware

- [x] You've read the [Contributor Guide](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CODE-OF-CONDUCT.md).
- [x] You've included unit or integration tests for your change, where applicable.
- [x] You've included inline docs for your change, where applicable.
- [ ] There's an open issue for the PR that you are making. (Perf finding, no separate issue.)

Stop re-scanning endpoint metadata on every request for endpoints without authorization metadata.

## Description

### Problem
When `AuthorizationMiddleware` is created with an `IServiceProvider`, which is the normal `UseAuthorization()` path, it caches the combined policy per endpoint in `AuthorizationPolicyCache`. It only caches **non-null** policies, though. An endpoint that has no `IAuthorizeData`, `AuthorizationPolicy` or `IAuthorizationRequirementData` metadata, in an app without a fallback policy, gets `null` from `AuthorizationPolicy.CombineAsync`. Nothing is cached, so **every request** to that endpoint:
- calls `GetOrderedMetadata<IAuthorizeData>()`, `GetOrderedMetadata<AuthorizationPolicy>()` and `GetOrderedMetadata<IAuthorizationRequirementData>()`
- runs the `CombineAsync` async state machine and calls `GetFallbackPolicyAsync()`

This is the common case for anonymous pages, static/public endpoints, health checks and similar routes in apps that call `UseAuthorization()`.

### Change
- When the combined policy is `null` and caching is enabled, store a private static marker policy in the per-endpoint cache. The marker is never evaluated. It's added only when the endpoint has nothing cached yet (`TryAdd`), so a delayed `null` result from an overlapping request can't replace a policy that another request cached.
- On a cache hit for the marker, the endpoint is known to have no authorization metadata, so the combined policy is, by definition of `CombineAsync`, exactly `GetFallbackPolicyAsync()`. That's still queried on each request while it returns `null`, and once it returns a non-null policy that policy replaces the marker in the cache. This matches the previous behavior, where a non-null fallback policy was cached the first time it was observed.
- Everything after policy computation is unchanged: `[AllowAnonymous]` handling, authentication, evaluation, challenge and forbid.

There are no public API changes. `AuthorizationPolicyCache` is internal and used only by `AuthorizationMiddleware`, so the marker can't be observed by callers. The cache key is the endpoint and the marker carries no user data. The cache is still cleared on endpoint data source changes as before.

### Benchmarks
New `AuthorizationMiddlewareCachedPolicyBenchmark`: `UseAuthorization()`-style middleware with a DI provider and `EndpointDataSource`, and an endpoint with 12 non-authorization metadata items. BenchmarkDotNet with `[MemoryDiagnoser]`, in-process, 3 warmup and 15 measured iterations, 3 interleaved A/B rounds, on the same machine:

| Round | main | PR |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 168.0 ns, 40 B | 85.35 ns, 0 B |
| 2 | 164.5 ns, 40 B | 90.56 ns, 0 B |
| 3 | 158.5 ns, 40 B | 85.23 ns, 0 B |

That's **about 47% less time per request and 0 allocations** for endpoints without authorization metadata.

Re-run after the `TryAdd` race fix (different machine, same settings, 3 interleaved rounds):

| Round | main | PR |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 132.2 ns, 40 B | 75.80 ns, 0 B |
| 2 | 130.2 ns, 40 B | 74.13 ns, 0 B |
| 3 | 138.3 ns, 40 B | 72.75 ns, 0 B |

That's still **about 44% less time and 0 allocations**.

### Tests
- New: `EndpointWithoutAuthorizationMetadata_WithCache_PicksUpFallbackPolicyWhenSet`. A fallback policy that starts out `null` and later becomes a deny policy is honored on subsequent requests to the same cached endpoint.
- New: `EndpointWithoutAuthorizationMetadata_WithCache_DoesNotAffectOtherEndpoints`. A cached "no metadata" endpoint doesn't affect `[Authorize]` endpoints sharing the cache.
- New: `EndpointWithoutAuthorizationMetadata_WithCache_DelayedNullFallbackDoesNotReplaceCachedPolicy`. A delayed `null` fallback result from an overlapping request doesn't replace a policy cached by another request. It fails without the `TryAdd` fix.
- `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authorization.Test`: **170 passed, 0 failed** (net12.0).
